archetype.name: Retooling (special-teams reliant)
archetype.definition: A Calgary side several years removed from its 111-point season that controls enough of the puck to look respectable but doesn't generate quality at 5-on-5, and currently leans on a top-five power play and close-game results to stay near .500.

report.headline: A near-.500 record built on the power play and close wins, not 5-on-5
report.take:
The Flames are 8-9-1 and fifth in the Pacific, which flatters them. Their Goal Diff / GP of -0.94 ranks 28th, they've been outscored 63-46, and only one team has collected more standings points beyond what its goal differential implies (Pts vs Goal Diff 2.5, 2nd). The site has them 23rd of 32, and the 82-game pace of 77 points matches last season's 77 exactly. Nothing here yet says this team is better than the one that finished 34-39-9.

The 5-on-5 profile is the core problem, and it is subtler than a bad possession team. Calgary takes 51% of the shot attempts (CF %, 11th) but only 46.9% of the expected goals (25th). It has the puck and does little with it: attempts from the outside, not chances. That shows up in the finishing, a 9.3% shooting rate that ranks 29th against a league average of 11.6%. Some of that is bad luck, since a 5-on-5 PDO of 96 is about as low as it gets. But a team with a sub-47% xGF share has earned some of its low conversion, so expect partial recovery, not a full one. Mikael Backlund has two goals on 41 shots, and the nine listed forwards have 34 goals on 312 shots. What has kept the offense alive is a power play converting 28.6% (5th), up from 16.2% a year ago, with Joel Farabee (9 PP points) and Matt Coronato (7) driving it.

The goaltending is the other story, and it is a two-man split. The past two seasons Calgary got strong goaltending (Goalies GSAx of 16.7 and 14.2). This year the team number is -4.2 (26th), and almost all of it belongs to Dustin Wolf: .869, a 3.75 GAA and -6.6 GSAx over nine starts. Devin Cooley has been the opposite at .914 and +2.4 in eight starts, 18th of 69 on the goalie tab. October's 52 goals allowed in 14 games reflects that split as much as any structural defensive flaw. Over the last 10 games Calgary allowed 2.6 a game, nearly a goal better than its season rate, and went 6-3-1.

So the trajectory is mildly upward, but on fragile supports. The power play will probably cool from 28.6%, and the close-game luck will probably fade. Shooting should tick up, and the goaltending can only improve if Wolf finds last year's form or Cooley keeps taking starts. The net is a team that can hover around .500 for stretches without having the 5-on-5 game to sustain a playoff push. The forwards and goalies both grade D and the blueline D+. Farabee (11th of 126 left wings) is the only skater ranking near the top of his tab.

strengths.title: A top-five power play
strengths.body: Calgary converts 28.6% of its power plays, fifth in the league and well above the 22.5% league average. That is a huge jump from last season's 16.2%, which ranked among the worst in the sheet's history. Farabee and Coronato account for much of it, and Zayne Parekh has five PP points from the back end. Some regression is likely given the leap, but it is the main reason a 29th-ranked offense isn't worse.

strengths.title: Penalty kill holding firm
strengths.body: The kill is at 82.1%, ninth in the league and above the 77% average, in line with the roughly 80-83% range Calgary has posted most recent seasons. Because it matches history, this looks real rather than a hot streak. Paired with the power play, special teams are the one area where the Flames win games.

strengths.title: Cooley giving them a chance
strengths.body: Devin Cooley has a .914 save percentage and +2.4 GSAx across eight starts, ranking 18th of 69 goalies. That is a different team from the one in front of Wolf. If his share of the net grows, the goals-against problem shrinks considerably.

concerns.title: Possession without chances at 5-on-5
concerns.body: A 51% share of shot attempts against a 46.9% share of expected goals means Calgary is losing the quality battle even when it has the puck. That gap is structural, not luck, and it is why the 9.3% shooting rate won't fully recover. Most of the forward group sits below even in xGF %, with Coronato at .42.

concerns.title: Wolf's collapse in goal
concerns.body: After two seasons of positive team GSAx, Calgary's goalies are at -4.2, and Wolf alone is at -6.6 over nine starts with an .869 save percentage. A small sample can swing back quickly, but until it does, every Wolf start is a game where the Flames need to outscore a leak. The goaltending grade sits at D.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the goal differential
concerns.body: Calgary's Pts vs Goal Diff is 2.5, second in the league, on a -17 differential. That is overtime points and one-goal wins, like the overtime result against Philadelphia and the 2-1 win in San Jose. It tends to wash out, which means the standings position is softer than the record makes it look.

trend.note: A rough October, with 52 goals allowed in 14 games, gave way to a 6-3-1 run over the last 10 that included a four-game win streak. The last five have cooled to 2-2-1 and a -4 differential, though even that beats the season rate.

weekAhead.headline: Elite Rangers goaltending at home, then two leaky California defenses
weekAhead.body:
The week opens with the hardest game. The Rangers come in 12th on the site with an A+ goaltending grade, a .911 save percentage (3rd), the second-best penalty kill at 89.1%, and just 23.2 shots allowed a game (4th). For a Calgary team shooting 9.3% and leaning on its power play, that is close to a worst-case opponent. Their forwards are held well under expected scoring (5th), so a low-event loss is the likeliest script.

The road trip is the opportunity. Los Angeles is 29th on the site with a league-worst 62.5% penalty kill and D- goaltending, and it gives up points to centers at the second-worst rate in the league. Anaheim, on the next night, allows goals at the 30th-ranked rate, stops just .869 of shots (31st) and gets out-chanced badly at 5-on-5 (44.2% xGF). The catch is that the Ducks own the league's best power play at 38.5% and shoot 15.4%, and they beat Calgary 5-3 a week ago. Back-to-back road nights also make it likely both Calgary goalies play.

keyMatchups.title: Calgary power play vs Kings' kill
keyMatchups.body: Calgary's 28.6% power play, fifth in the league, meets a Los Angeles kill that ranks last at 62.5%. This is the clearest edge of the week. A couple of power-play goals could decide it, since the Flames rarely win the 5-on-5 game outright.

keyMatchups.title: Ducks' power play vs Calgary discipline
keyMatchups.body: Anaheim converts 38.5% with the man advantage, best in the league, and shoots 15.4% overall. Calgary's 82.1% kill is good, but the Ducks' offense lives on finishing, so staying out of the box matters more than usual. In return, Anaheim's .869 save percentage gives Calgary's cold shooters their best chance to break out.

keyMatchups.title: Cold shooters vs Rangers' goaltending
keyMatchups.body: New York stops .911 of shots and allows 23.2 shots a game, while Calgary shoots just 9.3%. The Flames' habit of volume without quality is exactly what an elite goaltending team absorbs. Expect a low-scoring game in which a single power play could swing it, though the Rangers' kill ranks second.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal, and when. Cooley's .914 against Wolf's .869 is the biggest single lever on Calgary's results, and the back-to-back forces a split.

restOfSeason.body:
The season pace says 36 wins and 77 points, the same total as last year, and the underlying numbers support roughly that. Two things should lift Calgary: shooting can't stay at 9.3% with league-average shot volume, and Wolf's -6.6 GSAx is unlikely to persist at that rate. Two things should drag it back: a 28.6% power play is a big outlier against last year's 16.2%, and the second-best Pts vs Goal Diff in the league will fade toward neutral. The 46.9% expected-goals share is the anchor, and a team that loses the chance battle at 5-on-5 doesn't sustain a playoff-pace points percentage.

My range is 33 to 39 wins and 74 to 86 standings points. Reaching the top of that needs Cooley to hold up as the de facto starter, or Wolf to return to form, and the power play to stay well above average. Scoring should settle somewhere between 2.6 and 2.9 goals a game as the shooting normalizes partway. In a Pacific where Vancouver and Los Angeles are struggling, fifth place is reachable, but a playoff spot would take a 5-on-5 improvement this roster hasn't shown.
swingFactors: Wolf's recovery or Cooley's share of starts
How far the power play regresses from 28.6%

confidence.note: 18 games is a small sample, especially for goalie splits and shooting percentage, but the xGF and history picture is consistent.
